title: THE TIMEKEEPER
standing: An invented suspect. The history is real.

suspect.name: The Timekeeper
suspect.line: Wanted: for trying to wind the world back to 1788.
suspect.portrait_note: BK's Gemini illustration (22:11), placed by Josh with the prompt logged.
suspect.portrait_alt: An invented figure in silhouette, holding a pocket watch.
suspect.portrait_src: Illustration made with Gemini (AI) by Mr. Kelley. The suspect is invented.

intro: Someone is winding the clocks back.
The Timekeeper wants the world the way it was in 1788, before the French Revolution's ideas got out. Everywhere those ideas took root, he tried to stop the clock.
Follow his trail. Every place, date and document in this chase is real. He isn't.
At the end, you'll name the enduring issue that ties his trail together, and prove it.

stops.story: In 1789, France's National Assembly writes down that men are born free and equal in rights. The Timekeeper arrives too late: the words are already printed.

clue.text: Open the Enduring Issues map: The Declaration of the Rights of Man.

ask.stem: According to the Enduring Issues map stop, law is supposed to be the expression of what? Type it.
hints: Read what happened at the map stop.
Look for the word law.

question.stem: According to Document 3, which of these is one of the natural rights in Article 2?
options: Resistance to oppression
Choosing the king
Freedom from all taxes
Freedom from serving in the army
hints: Find Article 2.
Read the sentence that starts “These rights are…”
question.why: Article 2 names four natural rights: “liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression.”

stops.evidence: 1789 · Article 2: liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression · Casefile B, Document 3

stops.story: In 1791, the enslaved people of Saint-Domingue rise up against slavery. In 1804, Haiti declares its independence. The Timekeeper can't wind this clock back.

clue.text: Open the Enduring Issues map: The Haitian Revolution.

ask.stem: According to the Enduring Issues map stop, who declared Haiti independent in 1804? Type his last name.
hints: Read what happened at the map stop.
Look for the year 1804.

question.stem: Which of these is outside evidence for Documents 1 and 2: true, and not in either document?
options: In 1794, France's government voted to end slavery in all its colonies.
Toussaint wanted Liberty and Equality to reign.
The letter asks its readers to fight for the same cause.
Toussaint said his name was perhaps known.
hints: Three of these are in Document 1. Find them.
Outside evidence is true, and missing from the documents.
question.why: France's 1794 vote is true and in neither document, so it's outside evidence.

stops.evidence: 1793 · Toussaint calls his brothers to fight for Liberty and Equality · Casefile C, Document 1

stops.story: By 1812, Napoleon's reach crosses Europe and the ocean to Spain's colonies. The Timekeeper is one step behind.

clue.text: Open the Atlas: Central Europe in 1812. Look at the small map.

ask.stem: On the small map, which giant empire in the east stayed independent of Napoleon in 1812? Type its name.
hints: Find the color for independent states.
Look east of the Duchy of Warsaw.

question.stem: Based on Document 3, which event in 1808 led Spanish Americans to take control of their own local governments?
options: Napoleon placed his brother Joseph on the Spanish throne.
Spain freed its colonies after a war with Britain.
Bolívar had already freed all of South America.
The king of Spain asked the colonies to rule themselves.
hints: Find the year 1808 in the document.
Who ended up wearing Spain's crown?
question.why: Napoleon gave Spain's crown to his brother Joseph, and Spanish Americans refused a French king and took over their own local governments.

stops.evidence: 1808 · Spain gets a French king, and its colonies soon take over their own governments · Casefile C, Document 3

stops.story: Napoleon has been beaten. In Vienna, the winners redraw the map, and old ruling families take back their thrones. Every clock in the city reads 1788.

ask.stem: Who holds Lombardy and the city of Venice in northern Italy? Type the empire.
hints: Find northern Italy at the bottom of the map.
Match its color to the key.

stops.after: Austria takes back Lombardy and adds Venice. The trail has gone cold. But you can't wind back an idea.

stops.story: In 1846, Camillo di Cavour, a nobleman from Piedmont, writes that Italians must silence the small questions that divide them. The idea the Timekeeper buried in Vienna has come up again.

clue.text: Open the Atlas: The Unification of Italy, 1815–1870.

ask.stem: Italy's unification starts in the Kingdom of Sardinia, ruled from Piedmont. Which city is its capital? Type it.
hints: Find Piedmont in the top left.
Look for the city marked there.

question.stem: Casefile C asks: What did more to build Italy and Germany: agreeing to unite, or “blood and iron”? Which sentence is the strongest thesis for Italy, using Document 5?
options: For Italy, agreeing to unite did more, because Cavour argued that Italians had to silence the petty questions that divide them.
Cavour wanted Italy to be glorious and powerful.
Cavour wrote Document 5 in 1846.
Cavour uses the word emancipation.
hints: A thesis answers the question, and someone could argue with it.
Which one picks a side?
question.why: The first answer picks a side and gives a reason; the other three only repeat Document 5.

stops.evidence: 1846 · Cavour: silence what divides Italians · Casefile C, Document 5

stops.story: In 1862, Otto von Bismarck tells a committee of Prussia's parliament how Germany will be united.

clue.text: Open the Atlas: The Unification of Germany, 1815–1871. Look at the top map.

ask.stem: On the top map, which state's customs union grows into the German Zollverein? Type it.
hints: Read the first line of the top key.
Find Berlin.

question.stem: Document 6 (adapted) says the goal will be achieved “by blood and iron.” Which explanation best shows what that evidence means?
options: This shows he believed war and military strength, not democracy, would unify Germany.
This shows he wanted Germany to stay divided.
This shows he trusted voting to unite Germany.
This shows he planned to sell iron to other countries.
hints: What does he say will NOT reach the goal?
What could blood and iron stand for?
question.why: In the exam's version, “blood and iron” means war and weapons: Prussia fought Denmark, Austria and France, and in 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed.

stops.evidence: 1862 · Bismarck: blood and iron, not democracy · Casefile C, Document 6

stops.story: October 1912. The Balkan states are about to go to war with the Ottoman Empire, and Europe's great powers are trying to hold the lid on. The Timekeeper was here minutes ago.

clue.text: Open the Atlas: The peoples of Austria-Hungary, 1911.

ask.stem: According to the map, which people live in Bosnia? Type one of them.
hints: Find Bosnia in the south of the empire.
Match its color to the key. The map spells Serbs “Servians.”

question.stem: Which enduring issue does Document 8 best show?
options: Conflict
Economic Development
Cultural Exchange and Diffusion
Population and Migration
hints: What's about to boil over?
Check the Six Umbrellas: why people fight.
question.why: A pot about to boil over, with the great powers holding the lid, is Conflict; six days later, the First Balkan War began.

stops.evidence: 1912 · BALKAN TROUBLES about to boil over · Casefile C, Document 8
stops.nearMiss: You just missed him. He left a map open on the table: the peoples of Austria-Hungary. Bosnia is circled.

warrant: 1 · Set the scene. When and where? Use the years and places on your evidence cards.
2 · Name the issue. Which enduring issue shows up at three of your stops? Use its exact name from the Six Umbrellas card.
3 · Explain it. What does it mean? Say it in your own words. Stuck? Open the enduring issues list in the Arena. It's always there.
4 · Prove it. Pick one evidence card. What happens in that document that shows the issue?
5 · Prove it again. Use a different stop.

final.prompt: Which enduring issue do three of his stops share? Use its exact name from the Six Umbrellas card.
hints: Look at your evidence cards. What do stops 5, 6 and 7 have in common?
Check the Six Umbrellas card for the exact name.

pill.label: Enduring issues
pill.shows: the list of enduring issues and their definitions (the Six Umbrellas card)

final.callout: Learn these. They're on every Regents exam. Practice them anytime in the Arena: Enduring Issue, Level 1 (the matching game).
final.after: That's it. Now finish steps 3, 4 and 5 on your Case File.

lines: That's it. Every time he wound the clock back, the idea came back.
His trail ends in Sarajevo, in Bosnia. The Timekeeper is gone, and he never made history happen. People did.
On June 28, 1914, a Bosnian Serb nationalist shot the heir to Austria-Hungary's throne in Sarajevo.
A month later, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and Europe went to war. That's World War I, in Unit 10.5.
You can't wind back an idea. You can only follow where it goes.

reflection: Which question did you get right on the first try, and how?
At Vienna, the Timekeeper wound the clocks back. Why didn't it hold?
Which Arena tool will you use before Friday's essay, and for what?
